records.name: Olita
records.facts_used: Olita: Siliņš’s entry connects the name with Olga. Olga is an East Slavic form of Scandinavian Helga, based on helagr, holy or blessed. The chain matters: the Latvian form is linked to Olga, while the older explanation belongs to Helga. Siliņš’s dictionary dates the use of Olita: 1906. Its calendar year is 1915. This records use of the particular name in Latvia. The entry cannot automatically be transferred to similar spellings or treated as the moment the entire name family originated.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Siliņš pp254/253 exact form. Old Norse holy independently corroborated; no speculative Germanic healthy/happy route adopted.

records.name: Jokūbas
records.facts_used: Jokūbas: The Lithuanian form belongs to Hebrew Yaakov, transmitted through Greek Iakōbos and Latin Jacobus. In the biblical narrative Jacob is born holding his brother’s heel. That is a traditional explanatory story, rather than independent proof of the whole name’s literal etymology. In the essay reprinted in 1983, Salys describes Jokūbas developing from older Jakūbas. He mentions Jakubos and Jacobus in sixteenth-century inventories and the link to Polish and Belarusian Jakub. These are particular written forms, not a claim to the first registration of Jokūbas.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: PDF92 printed77 visually checked. Biblical heel story explicitly scoped as traditional narrative; no assertion that it proves a literal root.

records.name: Rimgaudas
records.facts_used: Rimgaudas: A Lithuanian two-stem name with rim-, linked by the guide to rimti, ramintis, to become calm, and gaud-, explained through gaudus, resonant. This is an explanation of components rather than an artificially combined description of a person. The 1964 calendar reprinted in Salys’s 1983 volume gives Rimgaudas (Rimas) on 28 November. This is a concrete printed example of the form’s use. Its position in the historical calendar need not match every modern calendar and is not the name’s invention date.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Guide stem gloss attributed; Salys PDF318 printed303 November28 confirms exact name and short form. No inferred compound sentence.

records.name: Rufas
records.facts_used: Rufas: The Lithuanian guide connects the name with Latin rufus, red or ruddy. Rufus was also a Roman cognomen. The colour word belongs to an older naming tradition rather than asserting the hair colour of every modern Rufas. The Dictionary of Medieval Names documents the related Latin Rufus in Belgium in 1050, citing a particular documentary edition. This shows the family’s written continuation after antiquity. The record does not date the first appearance of Lithuanian Rufas itself.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: DMNES Latin1050 Belgium CRS-2-5p232 belongs to related Rufus; not a Lithuanian first attestation.

records.name: Steponas
records.facts_used: Steponas: The Lithuanian form belongs to Greek Stephanos. Greek stephanos means wreath or crown, and the name spread through Christian tradition. Latin uses Stephanus, while different languages have preserved distinct forms. The 1964 calendar reprinted in Salys’s 1983 volume gives Steponas (Stepas) on 26 December. This is a concrete printed example of the form’s use. Its position in the historical calendar need not match every modern calendar and is not the name’s invention date.

records.name: Laima
records.facts_used: Leole explains the name used in Estonia by reference to Latvian. Latvian laime means luck or happiness, and Laima is also the name of a Baltic goddess of fate. The common word and mythological figure are connected without predicting a bearer’s future. Leili Kuusk’s column in the municipal newspaper Leole, November 2005, page 6, uses the exact spelling Laima. This local explanation documents the name in Estonian print culture. It is neither the name’s first registration nor its year of invention.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Leole supplies the exact dated Estonian spelling and explicitly refers to Latvian. Wiktionary has Latvian/Lithuanian sections only, not an Estonian entry; it supports the Latvian word and mythology, not an Estonian borrowing claim.
